meta.blurb: Arjuna drops his bow. Two armies wait, and he cannot fight the cousins and teachers he loves. His charioteer, Krishna, answers with a conversation about duty, fear and who we really are, at the heart of one of India's most loved texts.
meta.bible: Bhagavad Gita: a sacred text of Hinduism, 700 verses in 18 chapters; the name means the Song of the Lord. It is one small part of the Mahabharata, the great epic of ancient India, and is traditionally linked to the sage Vyasa. Arjuna: a Pandava prince and a great archer, brave but overcome by sorrow; Krishna's friend. Krishna: Arjuna's friend and charioteer, honoured in the tradition as the Lord himself in human form; speaks calmly, kindly and sometimes with a smile. Sanjaya: the minister who tells the whole story to the blind king, given the gift of seeing the battle from afar. Dhritarashtra: the blind king, father of the Kauravas. Kurukshetra: the plain where the armies stand. Pandavas and Kauravas: two branches of one royal family, cousins, whose armies are about to fight for the kingdom. Bhishma: the eldest and most honoured of the family. Drona: the teacher who taught Arjuna archery. Vivasvan: the sun god, to whom Krishna says he first taught this knowledge; Manu: the first lawgiver. Meru: the great mountain. Ganges: the holy river. India. Hindu. Hinduism. Sanskrit. Dharma: righteousness, the right order of things and a person's duty. Yoga: discipline, a way of joining the self with the divine. Gunas: the three strands of nature, Sattva (light, purity, calm), Rajas (passion, restlessness) and Tamas (darkness, heaviness, confusion). Self: the eternal self inside every being. Each beat is one step of the conversation, in the order of the chapters: Arjuna's despair (1), the self and duty (2), action (3), the ancient teaching (4), renunciation (5), meditation (6), knowledge (7), remembrance (8), the royal secret (9), glories (10), the universal form (11), devotion (12), the field (13), the three strands (14), the tree (15), the two natures (16), faith (17), freedom and surrender (18). Voice and tone: reverent, clear and calm; verses are paraphrased and never copied; respectful of the tradition and neutral toward other traditions; war is stated plainly and without gore; nothing is preached.

B1B2: The Bhagavad Gita is a holy book of Hinduism, made of 700 verses in 18 chapters. It forms one part of the great epic poem called the Mahabharata, and it is a conversation between a prince and Krishna.
The story begins on the plain of Kurukshetra, where two armies of cousins are ready for war. The blind king Dhritarashtra asks his helper Sanjaya to tell him everything that happens.
Arjuna, a brave prince and a great archer, rides in a chariot driven by his friend Krishna. He asks Krishna to drive between the two armies so that he can see who stands ready to fight.

Looking across the field, Arjuna sees his teachers, his uncles, his cousins and his friends standing on both sides. His heart fills with sadness, because he knows that many of them will not come home.
Arjuna tells Krishna that his legs are weak, his mouth is dry and his skin is burning. His great bow slips from his hand, and he cannot stand up.
Arjuna says that he sees no good in killing his own family, even for a kingdom. Putting aside his bow and arrows, he sits down in the chariot, filled with sorrow.

Krishna answers gently, and he says that this weakness does not suit a man like Arjuna. The wise, he says, do not grieve for the living or for the dead, for there is something in us that does not die.
Krishna teaches that the self within each of us is never born and never dies. Weapons cannot cut it, fire cannot burn it, water cannot wet it, and wind cannot dry it.
To help Arjuna understand, Krishna gives him a simple picture of changing clothes. Just as a person throws away old clothes and puts on new ones, the self leaves a worn-out body and takes a new one.
Krishna reminds Arjuna that he is a warrior and that defending what is right is his duty. He should treat pleasure and pain, gain and loss, and victory and defeat alike, and then do his duty.
Here Krishna gives one of the most famous teachings of the whole Gita. You may act, but you may not demand the fruit, so do not work only for rewards and do not give up work.
Arjuna asks what a person of steady wisdom is like. Krishna replies that such a person is not shaken by sorrow, does not crave pleasure, and is free from anger and fear.

Arjuna is confused, and he asks why he must act at all if knowledge is higher than action. Krishna replies that no one can stay without acting even for a moment, because the forces of nature keep everyone moving.
Krishna says that work done as an offering, without selfish attachment, sets a person free. He adds that even he works, because whatever a great person does, other people follow.
Arjuna asks what drives a person to do wrong, even against his will. Krishna answers that the cause is desire and anger, which cover wisdom as smoke covers a fire.

In the fourth chapter, Krishna says that he taught this ancient knowledge long ago to Vivasvan, the sun god. Over time it was passed down through kings, but then it was lost, and so he is telling it again to Arjuna.
Krishna makes one of the best-known promises in the whole Gita. Whenever goodness fades and wrong grows strong, he says, he is born again to protect the good and restore what is right.
Krishna says that there is nothing in the world as pure as knowledge. As a blazing fire turns wood to ashes, he says, the fire of knowledge turns all the bonds of action to ashes.

Arjuna asks whether it is better to give up action or to do it with the right attitude. Krishna says that both lead to freedom, and that one who acts without clinging is like a lotus leaf untouched by water.
Krishna says that the wise see all beings in the same way. They look with equal respect on a learned scholar, a cow, an elephant and a dog.

The sixth chapter is about meditation, and it begins with a lesson about the mind. A person must lift himself by his own effort, says Krishna, because the mind can be his best friend or his worst enemy.

Krishna compares a steady mind in meditation to a lamp in a place without wind, which does not flicker. He also advises moderation in eating, sleeping and resting, because yoga is not for those who go to extremes.

Arjuna admits that the mind is restless, strong and stubborn, and that holding it still seems as hard as holding the wind. Krishna agrees that it is hard, but says that it can be done through practice and detachment.
Arjuna asks what becomes of someone who begins the path with faith but does not finish it. Krishna answers that no one who does good ever comes to ruin, and that no honest effort is wasted.
In the seventh chapter, Krishna says that among thousands of people, hardly one strives for the truth. He says that he is present in all things, as the taste in water and the light of the moon.
In the eighth chapter, Krishna says that whatever a person remembers at the end of life, he reaches. Therefore he tells Arjuna to remember him at all times, and to fight.
In the ninth chapter, which Krishna calls the royal secret, he says that he accepts even the simplest gift. If anyone offers him a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water with love, he accepts it.
Krishna says that whatever Arjuna does, whatever he eats, gives or practises, he should do it as an offering. In this way he will be freed from the bonds of action and will come to Krishna.
In the tenth chapter, Krishna describes how his glory shines in all the finest things of the world. Among mountains he is Mount Meru, among rivers the Ganges, and among the seasons spring.
Arjuna asks Krishna to show him his divine form, if it is possible for him to see it. Krishna says that he cannot see it with his ordinary eyes, so he gives Arjuna a divine eye.

Arjuna sees the whole universe in Krishna's body, with countless mouths, eyes and arms and a light as bright as a thousand suns. His hair stands on end, and he bows with folded hands, trembling with wonder.

Krishna says that he is Time, which brings the end of worlds, and that the warriors will pass away in any case. Then Arjuna, shaken, begs to see Krishna's gentle human form again, and Krishna returns to it.
In the twelfth chapter, Arjuna asks whether it is better to worship God with form or without form. Krishna says that both paths lead to him, but the way of loving devotion is easier for most people.

Krishna describes the kind of devotee who is dear to him, and the list is long and gentle. Such a person hates no one, is friendly and compassionate, stays the same in pleasure and in pain, and is quick to forgive.
In the thirteenth chapter, Krishna calls the body a field. The one who knows the field is the self within, and to understand both is true knowledge.
Krishna then lists the qualities that, in his words, make up true knowledge. They include humility, honesty, patience, non-violence, respect for the teacher, cleanliness and self-control.

The fourteenth chapter describes three qualities of nature, called Sattva, Rajas and Tamas. Sattva brings light and calm, Rajas brings restless desire and activity, and Tamas brings darkness, laziness and confusion.
Arjuna asks how a person who has gone beyond the three qualities behaves. Krishna replies that he stays the same in praise and blame, and sees gold and clay as equal.
The fifteenth chapter shows the world as an ancient banyan tree, with its roots above and its branches below. Krishna says that it must be cut with the strong axe of detachment.

In the sixteenth chapter, Krishna describes two kinds of people, those with godlike qualities and those with ungodly ones. Fearlessness, purity, charity, truth and non-violence are godlike, while pride, anger and cruelty are ungodly.
Krishna warns that there are three gates to ruin: desire, anger and greed. A wise person gives up these three, and then he walks the path toward the highest goal.

The seventeenth chapter says that faith comes in three kinds, and so do food, giving and effort. The best gift, says Krishna, is one given without hope of return, at the right time, to a deserving person.
Krishna also describes the discipline of speech, which he treats as a form of self-training. Words that cause no pain and that are true, pleasant and helpful belong to this discipline.

In the final chapter, Arjuna asks about the difference between giving up action and giving up its fruits. Krishna says that duty, charity and self-discipline must never be given up, but should be done without attachment to the results.
Krishna says that it is better to do one's own duty imperfectly than to do another's duty well. By doing work that is suited to his own nature, a person finds peace and success.
Krishna says that the Lord lives in the heart of every being. By taking refuge in him with all one's heart, a person finds supreme peace and a lasting home.
After so many words, Krishna does not force Arjuna to accept any of them. He tells him to think about it fully and then to do exactly as he chooses.
Then Krishna gives what many readers call his final and most precious advice. Let go of every other support and take refuge in him alone, he says, and he will free Arjuna from all fear and sorrow.
Arjuna answers that his confusion has gone and that, by Krishna's grace, he has found himself again. He stands firm, free from doubt, and he says that he will do as Krishna has told him.

Sanjaya ends his report to the blind king, saying that where Krishna and Arjuna stand, there are good fortune and justice. He says that the wonderful talk he has heard has filled him with joy, and the Gita closes there.
C1C2: The Bhagavad Gita, whose name means the Song of the Lord, is a sacred text of Hinduism, made up of 700 verses in 18 chapters. It forms one small part of the Mahabharata, the great epic of ancient India, and it takes the shape of a conversation held on a battlefield between the prince Arjuna and his charioteer Krishna. Millions of people have read it for centuries, as a guide to duty, devotion and the search for inner peace.

The scene is the plain of Kurukshetra, where the armies of two branches of one royal family, the Pandavas and the Kauravas, stand ready to fight for the kingdom. Far away in his palace, the blind king Dhritarashtra, father of the Kauravas, asks his minister Sanjaya what is happening on the field. Sanjaya has been given the gift of seeing everything from afar, and it is through his words that the Gita is told to us.

Arjuna, the bravest archer of the Pandavas, rides into the field in a chariot driven by his friend and guide, Krishna, whom the tradition honours as the Lord himself in human form. As conch shells sound from both sides to announce the war, Arjuna asks Krishna to halt the chariot between the two armies. He wishes to look closely at the men who have gathered to fight, before the first arrow is loosed.

As Krishna draws the chariot between the lines, Arjuna sees that the men he must fight are not strangers at all, but elders, teachers, uncles, cousins and friends. Among them are Bhishma, the eldest and most honoured of the family, and Drona, the teacher who taught Arjuna his skill with the bow. A wave of sorrow passes through the prince, and he understands for the first time what the victory he longed for might cost.

Overcome by grief, Arjuna tells Krishna that his limbs are failing, his mouth is dry, his body trembles, and his skin burns as though with fever. The great bow slips from his hand, and he can no longer stand upright, for his mind seems to be spinning. What had begun as the pride of a warrior has become the confusion of a man who does not know what is right.

No victory, no kingdom and no happiness in this world can be worth the killing of one's own relatives, Arjuna declares, and he would rather be killed unarmed than raise his hand against them. With these words he lets his bow and arrows fall, sits down on the floor of the chariot, and falls silent. The first chapter of the Gita ends here, with the hero in despair and with all the questions of life still waiting to be answered.

Krishna answers with a gentle smile, saying that this weakness of the heart is unworthy of a man such as Arjuna and that he should stand up and put it away. You grieve for those who need no grief, he says, and yet you speak the language of wisdom, for the wise grieve neither for the living nor for the dead. So begins the long teaching of the Gita, which starts, strangely enough, with the question of what a person really is.

The self, Krishna teaches, is never born and never dies, and it does not come into being and then cease to be, for it is unborn, eternal and ancient. Weapons cannot cut it, fire cannot burn it, water cannot wet it, and the wind cannot dry it, because it is beyond all the things that can be harmed. Only the body, which is the visible dress of the self, comes to an end, and so there is no cause for the grief that fills Arjuna's heart.

To help Arjuna understand, Krishna offers a simple and homely image: as a person casts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the embodied self casts off worn-out bodies and enters others that are new. Death, in this view, is not an ending but a change of dress, and the one who wears the clothes goes on. This is not meant to make Arjuna careless of life, but to free him from a terror that was blinding his judgement.

Krishna reminds Arjuna that he is a warrior, and that for a warrior there is no higher duty than to defend what is right when the cause is just. He must prepare himself, the Lord says, by treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, and victory and defeat as the same, and then do what must be done. Duty performed in this way, with a level mind, does not stain the one who performs it.

Here Krishna gives one of the most famous teachings of the whole poem: you have a right to your actions, but never to the fruits of your actions. Let the reward not be your motive, he says, and yet let there be no attachment to inaction either, for the person who works without clinging to results acts with a calm that nothing can break. To be devoted to the work itself, and not to its outcome, is the heart of what the Gita calls the Yoga of action.

Arjuna asks how one may recognise a person of steady wisdom, and how such a person speaks, sits and walks. Krishna answers that he is not shaken by sorrow, does not hunger after pleasure, and is free from fear and anger, and that he draws in his senses as a tortoise draws in its limbs. Such a person is happy in himself, and that inner contentment does not depend on anything that others can give or take away.

In the third chapter Arjuna is still confused, and he asks Krishna why he must take part in such a terrible action if knowledge is said to be higher than action. Krishna replies that nobody can remain without acting even for a single moment, since the forces of nature drive every living being to do something. The real question, therefore, is not whether to act, but how to act, and with what inner attitude.

Work that is done as an offering, Krishna says, without selfish attachment, is what keeps the world in harmony and sets the worker free. He points out that he himself has nothing left to gain in all the three worlds, and yet he is always at work, for whatever a great person does, the rest of the people follow. Those who lead, in other words, teach more by their example than by their words.

Arjuna asks what drives a person to do wrong even when he does not wish to, as if some force were pushing him. Krishna answers that it is desire, which turns into anger when it is blocked, and that both are insatiable and very harmful enemies, covering wisdom as smoke covers fire and dust covers a mirror. The way to defeat them, he says, is to steady the mind by the self and to rule the senses from within.

In the fourth chapter, Krishna says that he first taught this imperishable discipline to Vivasvan, the sun, who passed it to Manu, who passed it to the royal sages, until in the long course of time it was lost. Arjuna is puzzled, since Vivasvan lived far earlier than Krishna, but the Lord explains that he has been born many times and remembers them all, while Arjuna remembers none. Because Arjuna is both his devotee and his friend, Krishna says, he is now giving him this ancient secret again.

Whenever Dharma declines and its opposite rises, says Krishna, he sends himself forth into the world, born age after age to protect the good, to put an end to evil, and to establish righteousness again. One who understands the divine nature of his birth and work, he adds, is not reborn after leaving the body but comes to him. The promise has comforted many readers, for it says that the world, however dark it appears, is never altogether abandoned.

There is nothing in this world as purifying as knowledge, says Krishna, and the one who has become perfected in Yoga finds it in time within himself. As a blazing fire reduces its fuel to ashes, so the fire of knowledge reduces to ashes the bonds of every action. Faith, he adds, belongs to the one who is devoted to it and who has mastered his senses, while the doubter, who has neither faith nor knowledge, is lost.

In the fifth chapter Arjuna asks whether it is better to renounce action or to practise the Yoga of action, and Krishna replies that both lead to the highest goal, though the Yoga of action is the easier. The person who offers his actions to the divine and abandons all attachment, he says, is untouched by wrong, as a lotus leaf is untouched by the water on it. His body, mind and senses work, but he works only for the purification of the self and does not cling to the fruit.

The wise, says Krishna, look with an equal eye on a humble scholar, on a cow, on an elephant, on a dog and even on someone whom society despises, because they see one divine spark in all. Such a person has conquered the world even in this life, for his mind rests in a calm that does not rise and fall with every change. In this way the fifth chapter turns the quest for peace into a way of seeing other people, not only a way of treating oneself.

The sixth chapter is about meditation, and it opens with a lesson about the self and the mind. Let a person raise himself by his own effort and never let himself sink, says Krishna, for the mind may be his best friend or his worst enemy. To the one who has conquered it, the mind is a friend, but to the one who has not, it behaves like an enemy, working against him at every step.

As a lamp in a windless place does not flicker, says Krishna, so the mind of a yogi who has stilled his thoughts remains steady while he practises meditation on the self. This calm is not found by extremes, he adds, for Yoga is not for the one who eats too much or too little, or sleeps too much or too little. To the person who is moderate in food, in recreation, in work and in rest, Yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow.

Arjuna confesses that the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate, and that to hold it back seems as hard as to hold back the wind. Krishna does not argue, for he agrees that the mind is hard to control and always wandering, but he promises that it can be held by steady practice and by detachment. The reply is honest and encouraging, since it grants the difficulty and still insists that the effort is worth making.

Arjuna worries about the person who starts on the path of Yoga with faith but whose mind wanders away before he reaches the goal, and he fears that such a person might be lost like a torn cloud. Krishna answers with great tenderness that no one who does good ever comes to a bad end, either in this world or the next. The seeker who fails, he says, begins again in better circumstances and goes on from where he stopped, so that no honest effort is ever wasted.

In the seventh chapter, Krishna says that among thousands of people hardly one strives for perfection, and that among those who do, hardly one knows him in truth. Yet he is everywhere, he declares, as the taste in water, the light of the moon and the sun, and the sacred sound in the sacred texts. Like pearls strung on one thread, all things in the universe are held together by him, the chapter says, and are at rest in him.

The eighth chapter turns to the moment of death, and Krishna declares that whatever a person remembers when he leaves the body is the state he reaches. Therefore, he tells Arjuna, you must remember me at all times and fight, with your mind and your reason fixed on me, and you will come to me beyond doubt. The teaching joins two things that seem far apart, an everyday life of duty and a heart that is always turned toward the divine.

The ninth chapter is called the royal knowledge and the royal secret, and its message is one of astonishing generosity. If anyone offers me a leaf, a flower, a fruit or a little water with devotion, says Krishna, I accept that offering of love from the pure of heart. No wealth, no learning and no ceremony is required, only sincerity, and so the way is open to the poor as well as to the rich.

Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give, and whatever austerity you practise, Krishna tells Arjuna, do it as an offering to me. In this way you will be freed from the bonds of action, whether good or bad in their results, and with your mind fixed on the path of renunciation you will come to me. Thus every ordinary act, from eating a meal to giving a coin, may become a form of worship.

In the tenth chapter, Arjuna asks Krishna to describe the glories by which he fills the worlds, and Krishna answers by naming the finest example in each class of things. Among mountains he is Meru, among rivers the Ganges, among seasons the flowering spring, and among the senses the mind. He adds that he is the beginning, the middle and the end of all beings, and that whatever is splendid, strong or beautiful springs from only a spark of his radiance.

In the eleventh chapter, Arjuna humbly asks to see the cosmic form of the one who has been speaking to him, if he is able to bear the sight. Krishna replies that Arjuna cannot see it with his ordinary eyes, and so the Lord gives him a divine eye, a power of sight beyond the human. What follows, in the words of Sanjaya, is the most astonishing vision in the whole Gita.

Arjuna beholds the whole universe gathered into one body, with countless mouths, eyes and arms, wearing heavenly garlands and dazzling with a splendour like a thousand suns rising at once in the sky. His hair stands on end, and he bows his head with folded hands, trembling with wonder, awe and a little fear. He sees the gods, the sages and all creatures within that form, and he understands that what he took to be a single friend is the ground of everything.

I am Time, the destroyer of the worlds, says Krishna, and the warriors on both sides will pass away in any case, so rise up, Arjuna, and be only the instrument. Shaken by what he has seen, Arjuna begs forgiveness for having treated his friend so casually, and he asks to see the gentle human form again. Krishna smiles, takes up his familiar shape, and calms the frightened prince, who feels that he has returned to himself.

The twelfth chapter begins with a practical question: is it better to worship the Lord as a personal God, or as the formless and unchanging absolute? Krishna replies that both paths reach him, but that the formless way is very hard for those who live in bodies, while loving devotion carries a person swiftly across the ocean of change. If you cannot hold your mind steady, he adds, practise, and if you cannot practise, then simply work for him, and step by step you will arrive.

Krishna describes the devotee who is dear to him, and the portrait is among the best-loved passages of the whole poem. Such a person hates no creature, is friendly and compassionate, free from the sense of I and mine, patient and forgiving, the same in pleasure and in pain, and content with whatever comes. Since the world is not afraid of him and he is not afraid of the world, he is free from the agitations of joy, anger and fear.

The thirteenth chapter calls the body a field, the place where the seeds of action are sown and the fruits are reaped. The one who knows this field, says Krishna, is the self within, the knower of the field, and to understand both the field and its knower is what the Gita counts as true knowledge. It is a quiet idea, but it changes how a person looks at his own life, as a play to be watched as well as acted.

Krishna then lists the qualities that, in his words, make up true knowledge, and the list is more moral than intellectual. It includes humility, freedom from pride, non-violence, patience, honesty, service to the teacher, cleanliness and self-control, along with a steady love of solitude and an even mind toward everything that happens. To the Gita, in other words, a person is not wise because of what he has read but because of how he lives.

The fourteenth chapter explains that all of nature is made of three strands, or Gunas, which bind the self to the body: Sattva, Rajas and Tamas. Sattva is the quality of light, purity and calm, Rajas is the quality of passion, craving and restless activity, and Tamas is the quality of darkness, heaviness and confusion. Every person is pulled by all three, Krishna says, and which of them rises at a given moment decides how he thinks and acts.

Arjuna asks how one who has risen beyond the three strands may be known, and Krishna replies that such a person neither hates light, activity or confusion when they come, nor longs for them when they go. He sits like one who is unconcerned, unmoved by the changing qualities, and he is the same in pleasure and pain, in praise and blame, and toward a lump of clay, a stone and a piece of gold. Such a person, says the chapter, has passed beyond the strands of nature and becomes fit to unite with the highest.

The fifteenth chapter pictures the world as an ancient banyan tree whose roots grow upward and whose branches spread downward, and whose leaves are the hymns of the sacred texts. Its shape cannot be understood from within it, Krishna says, nor can its beginning or end be found, and so it must be cut down with the strong axe of detachment. Then one must seek the place beyond, from which those who reach it do not return.

The sixteenth chapter sets out two kinds of nature, the godlike and the ungodly, and it does so as a mirror for every reader rather than a list of other people. Fearlessness, purity of heart, charity, self-control, truthfulness, non-violence, gentleness and forgiveness belong to the first, while arrogance, pride, anger, harshness and ignorance belong to the second. The first, says Krishna, leads toward freedom and the second toward bondage, and Arjuna, to his comfort, is told that he was born with the first.

There are three gates to the self-destruction of the soul, warns Krishna, and they are desire, anger and greed, so a wise person must give them up. The one who is freed from these three dark gates, he says, does what is good for himself and so moves toward the highest goal. Whoever ignores the teaching and follows his own whims, by contrast, finds neither happiness nor success nor peace.

The seventeenth chapter observes that faith takes three forms, according to a person's nature, and that so do the foods people enjoy, the sacrifices they make and the gifts they give. A gift that is given because it is right to give, without hope of return, at the proper time and place, and to a worthy person, belongs to the highest kind. One that is given grudgingly, or in order to be repaid, or to the wrong person, belongs to a lower.

Among the disciplines that Krishna describes in this chapter is the discipline of speech, which he places beside the discipline of the body and the discipline of the mind. Speech, he says, should not cause distress, and it should be truthful, pleasant and helpful, and it should be accompanied by the regular study of sacred texts. Calmness, gentleness, silence, self-control and purity of heart are the matching discipline of the mind.

In the eighteenth and final chapter, Arjuna asks Krishna to explain the difference between renunciation and the giving up of the fruits of action. Acts of sacrifice, charity and self-discipline should never be given up, Krishna answers, for they purify even the wise, but they should be done with attachment and the wish for reward set aside. This, he says, is the true renunciation, and it makes a person free without making him idle.

Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed, says Krishna, for the one who does the work that his own nature calls him to does not incur blame. Each person reaches perfection, he adds, by devoting himself to his own task as an offering to the one from whom all beings arise. Every kind of work, from a farmer's to a king's, can become worship when it is done in that spirit.

The Lord dwells in the heart of every being, says Krishna, and so the divine is never far from anyone, whatever his birth or work. Take refuge in him with all your heart, he tells Arjuna, and by his grace you will find supreme peace and an eternal home. Having said so much, he tells Arjuna that he has now explained a knowledge more secret than any secret, and that the prince should think it over carefully.

After so many words, Krishna does not command Arjuna to obey him, and that restraint is one of the most striking things about the Gita. Reflect on all of this fully, he says, and then do as you wish, as though the whole of the teaching had been laid before a free and thinking person to accept or refuse. A conversation that began in confusion thus ends with the choice placed squarely in the hands of the one who was confused.

Then comes the verse that many readers regard as the heart of the whole teaching: abandon every other support and come to me alone for refuge, says Krishna, and I will free you from all evil, so do not grieve. The promise is given to a man who was afraid of failing in his duty, and it answers his fear with trust instead of with another rule. Some teachers read it as surrender of the fruits of action and others as surrender of the self, but most agree that it is the summit of the poem.

Arjuna answers that his delusion is gone and that, through Krishna's grace, he has regained his memory and his clarity. I stand firm, he says, with my doubts dispelled, and I will do as you command, which is not the surrender of a servant but the decision of a man who now sees clearly what is his to do. The bow that had slipped from his hands in the first chapter is lifted once more, and the eighteen chapters have brought him back to himself.

The Gita ends as it began, with Sanjaya speaking to the blind king Dhritarashtra, and he says that he has heard this wonderful talk between Krishna and Arjuna and that it has filled him with joy again and again. Wherever Krishna, the lord of Yoga, is present, and wherever Arjuna, the archer, stands beside him, there will be good fortune, victory, prosperity and sound judgement, and that is Sanjaya's firm belief. For readers, the poem remains what it has been for centuries, a short conversation on a battlefield that has become a long conversation about how to live.
